Interviewer 1:	First of all I’d like you to go around the group and say who you are and what course you’re from and what placement you did to start of with.

Jessica:	Hi I’m Jessica, I’m doing industrial design and technology and I was on placement at [company] who make [product].

Michelle:	Hi I’m Michelle and I’m on civil engineering and I was on placement at [company].

Jill:	My name is Jill and I’m in civil engineering as well and I was with [company] on my placement.

Grace:	Hi I’m Grace and I’m doing industrial psychology and I worked at the same place as Jessica, at [company] in [town].

Chloe:	I’m Chloe and I’m doing mechanical engineering and I spent my placement working for [company] working for a place that inspects and repairs gas turbines.

Samantha:	I do civil engineering like these two, and I was in Cardiff working with [company] on a road job.

Interviewer 2:	I’d like you to all write down on a scale of one to five one being bad, five being good, how committed you feel you are to an engineering or design career based on your industrial placement.

Samantha:	One being a number.

Interviewer 2:	Yeah, one being, you really hate it, you don’t want to carry on in the industry, or five being you really love it and that’s what you want to do forever and ever.

Chloe:	Solely on that basis of your placement?

Interviewer 2:	Yes.

Jill:	does money taken into account

Interviewer 2:	pardon?

Michelle:	Money! Laughter.

Chloe:	you wouldn’t do it otherwise

[inaudible]

[?]: It must be really hard coming back after that [Laughter]

Erm, you can get sponsorship for that!

[inaudible]

Interviewer 2:	I’m just going to go around the group now and ask you what you put and why you put it, So I won’t start with Jessica, I’ll start with someone else… Chloe 

Chloe:	erm, I put three, just because the role that I was in gave me a good understanding of both engineering and business perspective. And, even though I don’t feel some of the hardcore engineering, like deep theoretical stuff, is suited to me, there’s so many other skills that are involved that I wouldn’t be totally put off going and working back in the industry. So there’s quite a lot of opportunities once, you are in there that you probably wouldn’t even realise if you hadn’t been put in that environment.

Interviewer 2:	If anybody feels, when people are saying their experiences, if anybody agrees/disagrees then they can just shout out. Say what they have in common. So, does someone else want to say what they’ve put?

Grace:	erm I put one, [laughter]. Err, my placement was ok but I didn’t do any design in the whole year and that’s kind of what I expected to be doing. I was put in an engineering operations team so, although I wouldn’t want to go into that area I quite like the sort of ‘R&D’ but not necessarily due to the placement.

Interviewer 2:	What does ‘R&D mean?

Grace:	Research and development, 

Interviewer 2:	Ahh. So, you haven’t been put off part of the path in a career in design?

Grace:	err, I think it’s that fact that I didn’t like the factory-based work. That’s not really what I want to do.

Interviewer 2:	Yeah, so your placement hasn’t influenced you?

Interviewer 1:	Did you get a chance to see like the process and design stuff going on?

Grace:	Not really I think that most of that stuff is sort of contracted out, but 

Interviewer 1:	so you didn’t really get an insight into that bit at all

Samantha:	Not really…no.

Michelle:	Err, I put three. It was a good experience and I met a lot of interesting people and nice people, but there are some erm.., turn-offs. That it’s erm how the [company?] works or maybe it’s just [company] I worked for or that department. But there are some things that disappointed me. I don’t know if I want to work there forever and ever and obviously it’s not the best career for money, but it would be an interesting one.

Jill:	Err, I’ve got a three as well. Erm, for the work that I was doing, I experienced a lot of repetition. Erm you go into office you do the same thing and use the same program, you know [bridge after bridge?] ‘cause I was in bridge team ,err, doing assessment. This was not something that I expected to do and was hoping to do errm this was not what I wanted to do. The reason that I got into civil engineering was because I want to build bridges, I mean real bridges like suspension bridges: that kind of thing [laughter] Yeah? That’s my dream, but when you actually go to a company and that’s not the kind of opportunity that exists. I mean, let’s face it, how many big bridges are being built, you know, throughout the world, not just in one country? It’s just a lot of assessment and repairs and a lot of that going on, so it’s a lot of repetition and… it’s not easy to find something exciting, you know something new that you can explore. That’s a bit of the turn off. But, nevertheless, I don’t mind going back.

Michelle:	errm, it sometimes feels like a job rather than a career. As time goes by. It’s not as exiting as it was when I first started anymore, I don’t know if you agree with me

Group:	nods, yes.

Chloe:	I found like, at the beginning, ‘cause everything was new, everything was like a bit more exciting and you kind of made the effort to get into things. Erm I did to some pretty mundane things throughout the year but I think the fact that I got through them and found a way to motivate myself through those kind of times it means that if I can put myself through that I can put myself through pretty much anything really. But I did have times where, as soon as I’d got the hang of things I was like, OK what’s next!? So I did have those ups-and-downs as well!

Grace:	I’d agree with that ‘cause I had to learn erm , I had to learn scientific experiments pretty much everyday and I’d never really experienced that before. Erm, so I think that challenge of learning something completely new and then becoming expert in it and then erm, [nods] you agree with that.

Jessica:	OK, I’m the same as Grace [laughter] who worked at the same place, but it’s just. I didn’t do the same job as Grace, I was I the R&D bit that she finds a bit more interesting but it still wasn’t what I expected. I thought it would be designing things and I really wasn’t so… I didn’t really enjoy it very much. I didn’t really get a lot from it I don’t think!

Interviewer 1:	Do you think that the company mis-sold the placement to you?

Jessica:	yes! Totally. Completely, they told us that we were applying for a packaging placement. We just thought. They rang us up saying that we’d got the job and we thought we’d got the job. But when we got there we were all in completely different roles weren’t we?

Grace:	I think there was only one packaging placement.

Jessica:	but when we got there we were all in different places and they employed eleven of us.

Jill:	sorry.., what’s a packaging placement?

Jessica:	it’s the design of the packaging rather than the products.

Jill:	Ok.

Michelle:	So they didn’t tell you what you were supposed to do?

Jessica:	we thought, when we applied we applied through the internet and got to a second interview. So, we just assumed that we were being interviewed for the packaging placement, and, when we got there, when we’d got the job, we were all in different kind of roles. I was right in at the beginning of the projects trying to think of new things to do and there were people in packaging and there was Grace’s side which was… yours was just after mine doing experiments 

Grace:	form the idea to the product: yes mine was the experiments kind of side. We’d do experiments before it went in to the factory to make sure it worked and they only targeted our course, specifically. So we obviously just assumed that it was design-based and there was never any mention that you might be somewhere else.

Interviewer 1:	Did you speak to anyone from the company?

Jessica:	we spoke to them about it pretty early on, didn’t we, but they were basically saying that if you had rang up when they offered you the job then you could have spoke to your manager who would have told you what you were doing. It was a bit misleading really. I mean it was good, I learnt a lot through it, but not anything to do with design at all

Interviewer 2:	no?

Jessica:	No! [laughter] I mean I learnt a lot about working for a big company and a lot about it going down the pan [laughter] that’s the site where we are, it’s closing down [laughter] so everyone lost their job whilst we were there and we just like, ooh this is great.

Interviewer 2:	Welcome to industry!

[laughter]

Jessica:	yep! Erm it’s made me know what I don’t want to do!

Grace:	I think it will be quite useful in the future ‘cause at least you can say that you have done something else apart from design ‘cause it was totally underrated.

Interviewer 1:	So has it put you off pursuing a design career, or has it made you realise that you don’t want to do what you were doing on placement.

Jessica:	err, I don’t know. I mean it has put me off slightly but I don’t think I wanted to do it anyway just because the amount of hours and the amount of work you had to put in to be a designer for what you get back is ridiculous. I mean I our tutors tell us all the time, when they were actually in the design industry being designers they regularly worked one hundred-hour weeks and the pay’s just crap and I don’t think I am really prepared to do that. I think I would rather do something, I mean I am looking at something in advertising now so it’s something completely different. But we can use our degree for that so, 

Interviewer 2:	so over to you

Samantha:	[presents card displaying 5 to cheers!] What happened was, I really didn’t know what to do and after I’d had a crappy time at a placement in-between my first and second year. So I went in having like no preconceptions of the whole thing. The first six months were quite good and then it kicked-off at Christmas and I was given quite a lot of responsibility and by the time I left I was the only person left in my department and I had to leave everything pristine and, do you know what I mean so it was brilliant I really enjoyed it and it’s what I want to do for at east the next ten years, at least. 

Interviewer 2:	what were you doing?

Samantha:	I was working on site at a bypass in Wales. So I was working with the structures team and I actually had three or four structures by the end which I had to keep and finish-off. So it was quite a lot of responsibility I think and err, it was really a good, a really good team: and they did treat me really well actually. I think with us it depends on what site you are given and what you have with you, because some people seem to have really bad placements and some people have really good placements so…

Interviewer 1:	do you think that you were the only person that was based on a site, in this group, do you think that makes a difference?

Samantha:	weren’t you on site?

Jill:	no I never got out office.

Samantha:	oh right, I think it does make a difference because when you are out on site it’s a lot more relaxed and you’ve got 

Interviewer 1:	do you think it makes the job more varied, maybe?

Samantha:	yes, as well as every day’s different and you’ve got all the stress and you’ve got concrete miners coming in left, right and centre and things like that. I think I have noticed that looking at guys that have done office jobs for the year.

Jill:	yes in the office they come back saying, well, it’s very, very boring, indeed it was. I mean, to be honest, even though some people say, ‘what are you an engineer?’ and they’ll say [inaudible] ‘oh you’re only one year off from becoming a proper engineer.’ But still, to be realistic we are, at the end of the day, we are still students: they can’t possibly give us a design to do. So it’s just a lot of repetition or some very basic things you know need to do like running programs or stuff like that. And, once they know that you have got the hang of it and they chuck it into your face day after day, you are doing the same thing. I mean, yeah, I can see that because we are not as trustworthy as the graduates because at the end of the day we are students. They just won’t let us have that kind of responsibility: who’s gonna, decide on the design? Because, they can’t let us design it and someone sign it off. That is just not procedure.

Interviewer 1:	does anyone else feel that they were treated differently because they were students?

Michelle:	I think I was sort of lucky because I have a second in charge of my team who gave me quite a lot of responsibility. There happened to be a project which we had to analyse a lot of data and do some work that – I would say you don’t need an engineer to do it – but I think I was one of the cheapest [laughter] employees in the office so they weren’t too… I know it wasn’t my main job but they would tie you into this and that and there were some interesting and funny moments but it would be conversations between colleagues of you spoke to someone from the local authority and you think they are funny or they are silly and you talk about it that’s it. That’s the good stuff from work but in terms of work: even as I’m graduate I think it could be quite boring sometimes.

Interviewer 1:	I was going to say, do you think that the job will be any different after you graduate or do you think you will you have the same experiences?

Jill:	well at the same time, me and a graduate started on the same day. Well basically erm, we did exactly the same thing and he did hold a bit more responsibility than I did. Like he was helping to write the ‘AIP’, which is called approval in principle which is the method statement, how you are going to carry out a project. Err, he was taken to meetings to meet the clients and stuff: I never got any opportunity to do that I would just run the same program and use the same Excel spreadsheet, day after day every day for the whole twelve months.

Samantha:	God!

[Laughter]

Jill:	actually nine months [Laughter] to start with I was in a really, really bad team, I cried, honestly, I cried my eyes out. Err, everyday I went into the office and I hadn’t got anything to do and no one bothered to speak to me or anything. I was in this team and it really, really put me off. Honestly I just sat there statically and, you know I hadn’t got anything to do at all. They wouldn’t bother because that team was so busy and to give me something to do they would have to teach me and they were like ‘forget about it! it would be quicker it I could do it myself.’ In the three months I was counting correspondence and putting the stamps and registering mail: you know I thought I do not need a degree to do this!

Interviewer 2:	someone with more experience would still be saying that.

[laughter]

Grace:	I had I similar sort of experience. I was in a team that I was in where I didn’t well not really mix with. But it was difficult because my manager worked abroad quite a lot. And, again it was that sort of ‘we’re really busy so you’ll have to get on with your own thing.’ But I do feel that I also had quite a bit of responsibility ‘cause it was like ’we need this sorting out now, erm, can you send me a report to Germany or something by Friday’ type thing. So I think I was given quite a lot of responsibility but I don’t know if that was different to the rest of the team cause it seemed like everyone had their own thing to do and they’re all getting on with it and you just have to fit in with it. 

Chloe:	I found that definitely, in the beginning, that erm there seemed to be a general, kind of atmosphere of looking down on students. Erm, I am not really one for looking down on anyone. So it was a case of the longer I was there, I was just proving myself through my actions and how I did my work. And as the time went on I was given quite a lot of responsibility and was kind of dealing with managers direct and stuff. Erm, it actually had the effect that they were probably crapping their pants at the end of the day ‘cause I was quite persistent and stuff. But, I found that the atmosphere was good in that it was flexible enough to allow you to pick up skills that you didn’t have before. I mean if you weren’t sure of anything then you could go and ask someone. I would say that the placement was good on that kind of aspect.

Interviewer 1:	did you feel like you had to prove yourself to people?

Chloe:	I don’t know if I’d phrase it as though I had to. I think I wanted to, to show that you should not really underestimate people like that. And, fair enough, we are students, but that means we are studying a degree and that means at the end of the day we are there to do a job and as long as we do that well that is all that should count really. So I think I definitely gave them something to think about. I don’t think that it was something that was just common to where I was working, though I think it could happen elsewhere as well.

Interviewer 1:	Do you think that you were looked down on because you were a student and did anyone feel like it might have been because they were a woman as well?

Chloe:	No, the sex thing not at all. It was actually a bit of a novelty, because, 

Samantha:	yeah

Chloe:	because, it was like, ‘oh my god she’s a woman and they wouldn’t mind helping you out. Like I said, if they looked down on me it was because I was a student. But, like I said that was in the initial stages and once I’d proved that I was there to just get on with it, I think that kind of barrier just went. It wasn’t even thought of. But, yeah, whilst I was there I got involved on the workshop floor, welding, all kind of things and I didn’t encounter any problems at all. So it was probably a good thing that I was a girl, actually. 

Interviewer 2:	did anyone else have that kind of novelty?

Grace:	It was when you are working in a factory. Most of the line-operators don’t expect to see a young woman walk in I think. Erm, not that they treat you any differently, I think, it’s just at first just a ‘uh?, ok’. Like I say sometimes it was good as a needle to get what you want

[laughter]

Interviewer 2:	was this the same on site as well?

Samantha:	yeah it was the same. And also with the student thing a lot of people didn’t know I was a student they just saw me as an engineer, another engineer. I mean there’s enough of them around anyway, so I never had that issue.

Interviewer 1:	did you have a job-title?

Samantha:	erm just structural student engineer.

Interviewer 2:	was that student or trainee in you title?

Samantha:	I think student was my title, but you don’t go around with title on your head, do you know what I mean? I mean I was on this big site and everyone just knew I mean I didn’t have a sign on me, that I was a structural student engineer. I mean I was just another engineer you can’t just tell age-wise can you and I mean we all look like we are in our twenties, so you know…., groovy. 

[laughter]

Chloe:	we didn’t have titles at all…

Interviewer 1:	were you introduced as a student to other people?

Chloe:	yes, they tended to make a big thing out of it. Erm ‘there are new students who are arriving’ or ‘the students’ or ‘we’ll get one of the new students to…’ And that was kind of the thing that rubbed me up the wrong way.

Samantha:	did you have [inaudible] one in every year, was it a common thing where you worked?

Chloe:	yep, ‘cause even after what I said I managed to achieve in that year I still had a graduate that was doing/just started their rotation there, once I’d left, still trying to look down on us as a student.

Samantha:	really?

Chloe:	so I didn’t really think much of that because it was only two weeks whilst she was there and I was there. And I thought you haven’t got a clue what’s happened over this past year. Erm, but I think I definitely got the respect of my colleagues there. There was a work force of about thirty office-staff: all different positions, not all engineers and things. So, 

Samantha:	I found that some of the graduates, you know people that had been graduated a couple of years were quite glad to meet someone in their age-bracket

Chloe:	yeah, it wasn’t all the graduates, all the graduates, but there were a few that still wanted to [hand motions downwards to signify being ‘put-down].

Samantha:	‘hey you’re three years younger than me’.

[laughter]

Interviewer 1:	Were other people introduced as students?

Jessica:	yeah, if we sent anyone an email or anything like, it would be that we would have to have our name and address at the bottom and it would be like JESSICA Cater, IP student. But my boss always encouraged me as to not introduce myself as that ‘cause he said that it doesn’t help.

Grace:	I think that it was quite obvious with us as well wasn’t it?

Jessica:	yeah

Grace:	because we were the youngest people in the office by a quite a long-way.

Jessica:	yes there was eleven of us and we used to all go to dinner together [laughter] and all sit chatting in the middle-of-the-day.

Interviewer 1:	OK, erm, what do any of you think that you might have learnt about engineering culture? things, well, engineering culture could be various things like the managerial style that you experienced, or working with other people [inaudible]

Samantha:	[inaudible] erm, if something went wrong it was never the engineers fault, but it was the lads on the ground who blamed the engineer and the foreman blamed. It was just… at the end of the day you would have to sort it out and, you know, everyone did, but 

Interviewer 1:	do you think that’s particular to site work. Or?

Samantha:	I dunno, is it?

Chloe:	no, not at all, I found that where I was as well. It was ‘well this has happened because so-and-so didn’t do this’ and this, and this, and this. And someone just needed to stop and take responsibility: at the end of the day it’s got to get done. Just get on with it. So I found a lot of this as blame-culture and the politics of it as well, that they like to hit you with.

Samantha:	what did you get it with the designers and the contractors? We had that, err maybe the design was wrong: therefore we got it wrong.

Chloe:	not necessarily on the same wavelength: but definitely the temporary staff as against the permanent staff. Ooh, it was nasty and you wanted to stay out of that one.

Interviewer 1:	did anyone else experience this?

Michelle:	well, there were politics but not that responsibility because the reports we do we sign our names and it will go through our manager and then he is the one who is going to authorise it. So, at the end of the day, it’s his responsibility. But the politics would be the management: in my case my manager was, he’s a nice person but he’s not a good manager, so [inaudible] I don’t know it it’s a consultancy thing, the people in my team or even the floor – because we have quite a few teams on the same floor – they just leave every one or two persons per model or sometimes[

Jill:	[everyone wishes she has a leaving duty?]

[laughter]

Michelle:	I went to Birmingham Friday because I have got a colleague leaving and next Friday I am going to Birmingham because another’s leaving, the another told me, ‘I’m thinking about leaving’. And then I’m knowing someone who is leaving but she tells me that it’s because of her boyfriend. But then, it’s the company that you want to stay and work with, that you feel loyal to. Not that you want to leave as quickly as that.

Jill:	I think it’s pretty much down to management. Because in my team, nobody wants to leave. Well my manger is just great, well he’s my second manager, because I went to complain, I made a big fuss about it because nobody would bother, you know why I was there, what I was doing for the first three months.

Samantha:	did you ring [placement tutor]?

Jill:	No.

Samantha:	you should have done because he would have sorted it out.

Jill:	yeah right, I actually went to speak to the group manager but, apparently. he was the biggest back-stabber in [laughter, inaudible] he was the most hated man in the office. I mean the office itself is quite a friendly environment – well I’m not saying everybody kisses and you know, but they are friendly enough to be friends with, anyway this guy everybody just hates him. He will promise you one thing in front of you ‘ahh, how’s it going? I’ll sort that out,’ you know and then he turns around and goes, ‘yes just give her anything.’ You know, in terms of mail registering, or you know, running to HA like thee times a day. That was part of my duty as well, so I actually went to a higher- level to complain. You know ‘I come here to learn and to apply my knowledge.’ I don’t come here to sit and get paid and you know stuff like that and then I was moved to quite nice team in [inaudible]. After that everybody in my new team was really very nice and the blame-culture, I’m not sure if it exists in the office, but certainly not in our team. If they find a problem they will bring it out and discuss it and no individual holds the responsibility because it is such a big project and if I am doing things and the guy sat next to me. If I have done the counts and he should be in a position to check my counts and see if they are wrong it’s not all down to me or him. You know, bring out the problem and it’s considered.

Samantha:	the problem is that when you’re on site that if that occurs it means that you’ve wasted six wagons of concrete or something like that because it’s a big-deal because you’ve wasted a fortune and you’ve wasted a week or two weeks of time. Doesn’t bare thinking about.

Interviewer 1:	does the blame culture depend then on the type of place you are working at then?

Michelle:	definitely.

Interviewer 1:	and the people you work with: is that more important than the type of work you are doing or are they both important?

Chloe:	I think, probably, the people because you could be doing the world’s worst job, but as long as you have got a good set of people you can motivate each other and get through it.

Samantha:	that’s like every job though.

Chloe:	exactly, I don’t think it’s that specific to just the engineering industry, it could be anywhere.

Samantha:	you guys must find that I mean you’ve been working and that and stuff.

Michelle:	yes but don’t blame me as I don’t blame you either [unclear].

Interviewer 2:	yes, I mean there’s the kind of office politics/ factory politics. Do you think there is anything specific to engineering, or engineers?

Samantha:	well where I was there was about five different companies working: the designers, the council, the contractors, the sub-contractors, you had a lot of people trying to work together in a team and yet still – we’re trying to save as much money as we can - without paying the ‘subbies’ if we don’t have to, so if they screwed up they, you know what I mean and I don’t think that’s common to wherever everyone else works, you know what I mean.

Interviewer 1:	there isn’t exactly a loyalty because you are not all working for the same people.

Samantha:	exactly.

Interviewer 1:	because everyone’s loyalties lie in different places.

Samantha:	exactly, so they say you are a team, you are not really, you are all just trying to get the job done. 

Chloe:	I said I did spend some time on site, when they were like repairing cable lines and stuff and I did notice that as well. 

Interviewer 1:	do the politics issues put you off going into industry at all?

Jill:	politics comes into everything: you might as well just stay at home.

[laughter]

Chloe:	I think from the year out the only thing I would say is the only difference is where you work. You are going to find the same things everywhere, it might be a different strain, it might like tick you off and you thin, oh I’m gonna move and work somewhere else, you’ll find a different strain of it somewhere else: it doesn’t matter. So I think that it is important the you do something that interests you and something that is going to make you happy and then

Interviewer 2:	get out.

Chloe:	yeah, that sort of thing because I just think it’s everywhere.

Interviewer 2:	was it quite a male dominated culture or a female dominated culture between them or what?

Chloe:	you could definitely tell that there was a boy’s network going on [laughs] definitely, but, you didn’t feel excluded if that makes sense.

Interviewer 1:	so what do you mean by boys?

Michelle:	what activities: do they go to the gym together, or watch cricket together or play squash: something like that? They might ask you ‘do you want to come along?’ but you say ‘I don’t wanna play.’

[laughter]

Interviewer 2:	did they ask you as if the were expecting you to come or were they asking you knowing that ‘she won’t want to come’?

Michelle:	well, depends on the situation: invitations were like ‘oh, do come along and this and that’ or some of them would be like ‘oh, would you like to come with us? No! [laughter] or some of them would be football team and things like that. And there was a women football team or something like that just for fun: that they do invite the female. [inaudible] [laughter]

Chloe:	I think though that the industry’s been so used to just having males, they are just used to, I mean it’s like boy playtime, let’s just get our Action Men out. They are just used to being around each other. And like so, you didn’t really feel excluded. But 

Samantha:	they did try and shock me a few times by getting their phones out and showing pictures. I’m not going to try and describe them to you because the video is on! [laughter] well they would try and shock you and I was like ‘am I bothered?’ I have seem much worse than that, but no… but it was a novelty at the end of the day. And they didn’t really act that differently, they still swore as much and they would apologise, then they would carry on. Right! [laughter] yeah it was quite funny.

Interviewer 1:	did you ever feel like, not like the necessarily meant to exclude you, but, because you didn’t like cricket or whatever, did you feel like there was work related stuff going on in playtime where you might get left out and stuff, by default? Does that make sense?

Michelle:	no not at all.

Interviewer 2:	you never felt like you should go to cricket and pretend to like it?

Michelle:	no, in that case I would have invited them to go shopping with me!

[laughter]

Interviewer 1:	did you have experience of these boys’ networks going on?

Jessica:	not really there wasn’t that much going on.
